## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessed before the possessor; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; numeral before the noun; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-final.
It has a definite article before the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), singular, dual and plural, a gender system based on sex.
Verbs mark past and perfective; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator after the verb; yes/no questions use intonation alone. Verbs agree with the subject by prefixes; not with the object.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; alienable and inalienable possession told apart; verb reduplication; a periphrastic causative; a periphrastic passive; question words left in place; a decimal counting base.
Measured morphology: 19 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.2 (0 free word … 3 fused), 52 paradigm cells, 2 of them with allomorphy.

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (ʃi), 'at' (ɗoːɗa˯eː), 'with' (pi) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns fall into genders by sex: class 1 for men, and by default most other nouns, a separate word before the noun (kɑa˯, from 'man'); class 2 for women and female beings, a clitic before the noun (sa˯ʃũ, from 'woman').

| *kɑa˯* | *pa˯* |
| --- | --- |
| M | father |

‘father’

| *sa˯ʃũ=ɡulaː˯de* |
| --- |
| F=mother |

‘mother’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a suffix (ɾã˯, from 'yesterday'); perfect (PRF): a separate word after the verb (ŋuw‼ɑŋ, from 'hold'). Unmarked: future, progressive, habitual (left to context).

| *kʼeːʒa˯-ɾã˯* |
| --- |
| go-PST |

‘(it) went’

| *kʼeːʒa˯* | *ŋuw‼ɑŋ* |
| --- | --- |
| go | PRF |

‘(it) has gone’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 1SG: a clitic before the verb (ka˯, from 'I'); 2SG: a prefix (kʼu, from 'thou'); 3SG: a clitic before the verb (ɡɑʃwoːh, from 'he'); 1PL: a prefix (kɑ, from 'person'); 2PL: a prefix (ɓeː, from 'you'); 3PL: a prefix (ku, from 'they'). Subject pronouns are dropped when the marker is there.

| *ka˯=kʼeːʒa˯* |
| --- |
| 1SG=go |

‘I go’

| *kʼu-kʼeːʒa˯* |
| --- |
| 2SG-go |

‘you go’

| *ɡɑʃwoːh=kʼeːʒa˯* |
| --- |
| 3SG=go |

‘he/she goes’

**Negation.** Negation is a suffix (koː, from 'nothing').

| *ã˯tʃʼ-tsʼul‼oː* | *ka˯=tʼehli-koː* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-milk | 1SG=drink-NEG |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use rising intonation alone. Question words stay where the questioned phrase would stand: who le, what ɡul‼i, where kur‼u, when ɡul‼ipeː, how suji.

| *ã˯tʃʼ-ʃiʃʃaː˯ʃa˯* | *kʼu-sukulu* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-thunder | 2SG-hear |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *ã˯tʃʼ-ʃulã˯* | *ɡul‼i* | *ɡɑʃwoːh=kepiwdʒi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-child | what | 3SG=bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *ã˯tʃʼ-ʒeː* | *tʼehli* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-fish | eat |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands after the possessed noun, with no marker. Kin and body parts (inalienable) take no genitive marker. 'Having' is said with 'with' ('my mother is with a boat').

| *ʒu* | *ã˯tʃʼ-sul‼idʒitʼi* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | DEF-man |

‘the man's dog’

| *sa˯ʃũ=ɡulaː˯de* | *ka˯* | *kujieː* | *pi* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F=mother | 1SG | boat | with |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *sa˯ʃũ=wã˯tʃʼ-sa˯ʃũ* | *ã˯tʃʼloː* | *ɡɑʃwoːh=sidʒeː* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| F=DEF-woman | REL | 3SG=dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** There is no copula: a predicate noun stands beside its subject.

| *ã˯tʃʼloː* | *sul‼idʒitʼi* | *ka˯ww‼a˯* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| that | man | merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *ã˯tʃʼ-kuwedʒeː* | *diːket̪ʼa˯* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-water | cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Voice.** The passive is a clitic after the verb (ɓur‼a˯peː, from 'become'): the object of the active verb becomes its subject and the doer is left out.

| *ã˯tʃʼ-ʒeː* | *ɡɑʃwoːh=siŋe=ɓur‼a˯peː* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF-fish | 3SG=see=PASS |

‘The fish is seen.’ (sentence 13 below)

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action going on (CONT), by copying the whole stem.

| *kʼeːʒa˯-kʼeːʒa˯* |
| --- |
| CONT-go |

‘(an action going on)’

| *ã˯tʃʼ-sul‼idʒitʼi* | *ã˯tʃʼ-ʒeː* | *ɡɑʃwoːh=tʼehli-tʼehli* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-man | DEF-fish | 3SG=CONT-eat |

‘The man is eating the fish.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Giving (two objects).** Double object: theme and recipient both unmarked.

| *sa˯ʃũ=wã˯tʃʼ-sa˯ʃũ* | *ʒeː* | *ã˯tʃʼ-ʃulã˯* | *sa˯ʃũ=duhpaː˯lu* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F=DEF-woman | fish | DEF-child | F=give |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units; six to nine are built on five ('five one' for six). Twenty is seʒji and a hundred is l‼upkʼĩu.

| *tɬʼuloːldʒie* |
| --- |
| 6 |

‘6 = 5 + 1 ('five' and 'one')’

| *kujie* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *siŋutɬʼuloːl* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

**Concord.** The noun's class marker is copied onto the verb (subject concord) (agreement in class, as in Bantu and in Indo-European gender).

| *ʒu* |
| --- |
| dog |

‘dog’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *ã˯tʃʼ-sul‼idʒitʼi* | *ã˯tʃʼ-ʒu* | *ɡɑʃwoːh=ʒuli* | *ɡɑʃwoːh=ʒa˯ulu* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-man | DEF-dog | 3SG=sleep | 3SG=say |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count three distances: 'this' ɗur‼uldaː˯ (near), 'that' ã˯tʃʼloː (further) and a far one, a separate word before the noun phrase (ã˯tʃʼloːsi, from 'that'; 'that' with a place word grown onto it, as English 'that there' became 'yon').

| *ɗur‼uldaː˯* | *ʒu* |
| --- | --- |
| this | dog |

‘this dog’

| *ã˯tʃʼloː* | *ʒu* |
| --- | --- |
| that | dog |

‘that dog’

| *ã˯tʃʼloːsi* | *ʒu* |
| --- | --- |
| DIST | dog |

‘that dog over there (yon)’

**Comparison.** A locational comparison: the standard takes the word for 'at' ('big at B'), as Swahili kuliko 'where there is'.

| *ã˯tʃʼ-sul‼idʒitʼi* | *ã˯tʃʼ-ʒu* | *ɗoːɗa˯eː* | *lũ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF-man | DEF-dog | at | big |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 17 below)

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 2 families of 3+ words; 9% of the 725 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **path** *kleklupeː* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the silver dragon proto-language); 3 words have it as their main root, 3 contain it.

| meaning | IPA | spelling | roots (main first) | how it was built |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bridge | ŋiʒikule | ngizhikule | path, river | \*kle 'foot' (the silver dragon proto-language, 20 kyr) → … → colexified with PATH + 'place' = 'road' (20) → ROAD + RIVER = 'bridge' (1.5) |
| path | kuleːlupeː | kuleelupee | path | \*kle 'foot' (the silver dragon proto-language, 20 kyr) → FOOT + 'do' = 'walk' (20) → WALK + 'place' = 'path' (20) |
| road | kuleːlupeː | kuleelupee | path | \*kle 'foot' (the silver dragon proto-language, 20 kyr) → FOOT + 'do' = 'walk' (20) → colexified with PATH + 'place' = 'road' (20) |

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 55 families of 3+ words; 50% of the 725 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **fire** *delu* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the silver dragon proto-language); 7 words have it as their main root, 7 contain it.

| flame | delu | delu | fire | \*delu 'flame' (the silver dragon proto-language, 20 kyr) |
| red | soːŋdelu | soongdelu | fire | \*delu 'fire' (the silver dragon proto-language, 20 kyr) → FIRE + 'like' = 'red' (20) |
| roast or fry | deluːlu | deluulu | fire | \*delu 'fire' (the silver dragon proto-language, 20 kyr) → FIRE + 'do' = 'roast or fry' (20) |

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are one meaningful word; the byname is an inherited clan name, family name first. The tradition goes back to the silver dragon proto-language.

## Gods and liturgy

**Faith.** The mountain schism of the earliest silver dragons of Ratal, founded 250 kyr ago ago, held by 9 languages.

| spirit of the mountains | **Pulsiri** | /pulsiɾi/ | 'Mountain' | Pultsudu (silver dragon 17) |
| spirit of the open sky | **K'eesudziwrhkaamh** | /kʼeːsudz̪iw‼kaː˯/ | 'roof of the world' | K'eesidziwrhtaamh (silver dragon 17) |
| spirit of the hunt | **Ngeesamh'dsee** | /ŋeːsa˯ɗseː/ | 'the hunter' | Neesamh'dsee'd (silver dragon 17) |

How the first name came about: 'lord of the mountain' (a title) in p85, 20 kyr ago.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
